blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: State the reasons governments levy taxes, explain why taxation is the main source of government revenue, and keep direct and indirect taxation apart.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: What a tax is, and why it exists
blocks.text: A tax is a compulsory payment to a government, levied on income, spending or wealth, owed whether or not the payer receives any specific service in return. Taxes exist first to raise the revenue that pays for public spending: without them the budget would fund nothing. In Portugal a household meets them twice over - income tax on the payslip, value-added tax on the shopping bill - and both feed the same public accounts.

blocks.heading: Taxation as the main source of revenue
blocks.text: Of all the ways a government raises money, taxation raises by far the largest amount, and the reason is its reach. A tax is compulsory and falls on the incomes, spending and profits of the whole economy, so even modest rates applied to so large a base yield large sums every year. In Namibia, income tax on individuals and companies, value-added tax and the country's share of the customs and excise duties pooled by the Southern African Customs Union together provide the great majority of the revenue in each budget. The other sources are smaller or less reliable. Fees and charges, such as those for passports and vehicle licences, cover the cost of particular services rather than funding the budget as a whole. Profits paid to the government by state-owned enterprises tend to be small and rise and fall with those firms' trading. Selling a state asset, such as a share in a state-owned company, raises money once. Grants from foreign governments vary from year to year. Borrowing fills gaps, but it is not revenue at all: it is a debt that must be repaid with interest out of later budgets. In the United Kingdom, too, taxes on income, spending and profits provide the great majority of government receipts. So a government that wants to spend more year after year is, in the end, deciding how much tax to raise.

blocks.heading: Beyond revenue
blocks.text: Taxation also redistributes: a tax that takes a larger share of high incomes than of low ones transfers spending power towards poorer households, and the grants it funds do the same. And it corrects prices: a duty on tobacco makes the price carry more of the harm smoking imposes on others - the clinic time, the chest cases - steering buying away from a demerit good whose market price leaves that harm uncounted.

blocks.heading: Direct is not indirect
blocks.text: A common mistake is to treat every tax as one undifferentiated charge. A direct tax is levied on income or profit and paid straight to the revenue authority by the person or firm taxed; an indirect tax is levied on spending and collected by the seller, who adds it to the price and passes it on. To sort a tax, ask what the charge falls on - income or spending - and who hands it over: the taxed party itself, or a trader collecting it from buyers.
